# Arson Charges and Defense in Federal Fire Investigations

---

---

Federal arson charges depend on the property's federal connection, the cause of the fire, and proof of the required mental state.

A wildfire alone does not establish guilt. Prosecutors must connect the accused to the alleged ignition and prove the charged statute's elements using reliable evidence.

## 1. When Federal Fire Investigations Lead to Arson Charges

  

Federal jurisdiction depends on the property and statute. A fire on federal land does not satisfy every arson provision.

  

### Federal Property and Public Land Offenses

18 U.S.C. § 844(f)(1) covers malicious fire damage or attempted damage to federal property or property of certain federally assisted institutions.

Section 1855 separately prohibits willful, unauthorized burning of vegetation on specified federal and tribal lands. Land records and fire boundaries help establish which statute applies.

### Interstate Commerce and Special Federal Jurisdiction

Section 844(i) covers property used in interstate or foreign commerce or activity affecting commerce. Under *Jones v. United States*, a noncommercial owner-occupied home does not qualify solely through utilities or insurance.

Section 81 applies within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction defined by 18 U.S.C. § 7. Federal ownership alone is insufficient.

## 2. Evidence Used in Federal Arson Investigations

  

Fire-origin findings must be distinguished from proof of the accused's conduct and intent.

| Evidence | Issue to Examine |
| --- | --- |
| Origin-and-cause reports | Ignition location and competing explanations |
| Scene photographs and fire patterns | Fire spread and scene alteration |
| Debris testing and laboratory reports | Ignition materials and analytical limits |
| Surveillance, phone, and location data | Actions and chronology |
| Witness statements | Observation and consistency |
| Land records and custody logs | Jurisdiction and evidence integrity |

### Fire Origin, Ignition Sources, and Forensic Reports

NFPA 921 guides systematic analysis of ignition sources, fire patterns, and evidence handling; it is not a criminal statute. Suppression efforts and disturbed debris may limit findings.

### Witness Statements, Digital Records, and Physical Evidence

Witness accounts and device records require comparison with the physical timeline.

On October 9, 2026, DOJ announced a criminal complaint against Rodney Ameile Saba concerning the Bouquet Fire, which burned about 1,048 acres of federal land.

U.S. Forest Service investigators concluded that fireworks probably caused the fire after excluding alternative ignition sources. The allegations do not establish guilt.

## 3. Challenging Malice, Causation, and Fire Investigation Findings

  

The defense can contest conduct, mental state, causation, and forensic reliability.

# Ontario man charged with arson for Brogan Canyon Fire in eastern Oregon

Makenzie Stamets

Salem Statesman Journal

July 31, 2026, 8:29 a.m. PT

A 61-year-old Ontario man was charged with multiple counts of second-degree arson in connection to Brogan Canyon and Huntington Road fires on July 21, Malheur County Sheriff's Office said in a news release.

The man was arrested the night of July 21 and arraigned the next day on 15 counts of second-degree arson. His bail was set at $750,000 and he was being held at the Malheur County Jail.

# Man accused of setting eastern Oregon wildfires seeks reduction of $750,000 bond

* Updated: Aug. 13, 2026, 10:25 a.m.
* Published: Aug. 13, 2026, 10:03 a.m.

A cockpit view from a U.S. Air Force Reserve C-130H Hercules shows smoke from the Cow Camp complex fire as the aircraft provides aerial firefighting support in eastern Oregon, about 25 miles northwest of Vale near the Baker-Malheur county line, on July 21, 2026.Courtesy of the U.S. Air Force Reserve’s 302nd Airlift Wing

By 

* Tarek Anthony | The Oregonian/OregonLive

A Malheur County man accused of intentionally setting a series of fires that burned thousands of acres of Bureau of Land Management land was indicted last week on nine counts of arson.

A grand jury indicted Paul Emerson, 61, of Ontario, on nine counts of first-degree arson for allegedly setting fires near Lytle Road on at least six different dates between the beginning of June and his arrest on July 22.

Prosecutors allege Emerson set four fires the day before his arrest, the largest of which burned more than 6,000 acres and forced local evaucations. The fires were in the area of the Cow Camp Complex, which burned more than 8,000 acres of BLM land. Emerson is accused of causing hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage to public lands.

Emerson had been scheduled to enter a plea in Malheur County court Wednesday, but the proceedings were postponed. He is now scheduled to enter a plea Sept. 9 and is due back in court Friday for a hearing on his request to reduce his $750,000 bond.

Emerson was arrested in July and initially charged with 15 counts of second-degree arson for allegedly setting fires on the BLM land near Vale in the far eastern part of the state.

At the time of his arrest, Emerson worked one day a week as a delivery driver for the Argus Observer, a local newspaper in Ontario, according to a release recommendation report obtained by the Oregon Roundup Foundation through a public records request.

The Argus Observer initially reported that Emerson was an employee of the newspaper. The newspaper did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.

“The Malheur County Sheriff’s Office recognizes the significant damage these fires have caused our community and appreciates the public’s support and patience throughout this process,” the agency wrote following Emerson’s arrest.
